citation: Bussière, Chinn, Ferrara, Heipertz (2022), The New Fama Puzzle, IMF Economic Review 70(3); NBER WP 24342
main_claim: The forward-premium puzzle in eight USD pairs holds before the financial crisis but reverses afterwards (Fama coefficient large and positive)
mechanism: Change in co-movement of expectation errors and interest differentials; survey expectations support UIP more consistently
supporting_evidence: Eight USD exchange rates; survey expectations
methodology: Fama-coefficient analysis (method named only implicitly in the abstract)
limitations: Abstract only; sample period not stated on the page
sample_period: not stated on the page read (pre- vs post-crisis split)
testability: Testable on single pairs; regime split around 2008
data_needed: Daily rates and rate differentials (have: FRED H.10, DTB3, JGB)
publication_vs_sample: Post-crisis reversal documented before our validation window; our validation lies in the authors' 'new puzzle' period

citation: Brunnermeier, Nagel, Pedersen (2008), Carry Trades and Currency Crashes, NBER Macroeconomics Annual 23; NBER WP 14473
main_claim: Carry-currency moves are negatively skewed because carry trades unwind suddenly when risk appetite and funding liquidity fall
supporting_evidence: Funding-liquidity measures predict exchange-rate movements; panel regressions on futures positions, skewness, risk reversals, VIX, TED spread
methodology: Model with funding-liquidity constraints; empirical skewness and predictors (details not on the page)
limitations: Full text read in part; the October 7-8 1998 USD/JPY drop is presented as a move without fundamental news, and its link to carry unwinding is the authors' conjecture
sample_period: weekly 1992-2006 (risk reversals 1998-2006); AUD, CAD, JPY, CHF, GBP, EUR
testability: Risk-off filters (VIX, FX volatility) on carry exposure

citation: Engel, Kazakova, Wang, Xiang (2022), A Reconsideration of the Failure of Uncovered Interest Parity for the U.S. Dollar, Journal of International Economics; NBER WP 28420
main_claim: Interest differentials are a fragile, unstable predictor of USD excess returns and lose all power near the zero lower bound; y.o.y. inflation differentials do predict excess returns from the mid-1980s
mechanism: Markets underreact initially to predictable future monetary-policy changes (authors' interpretation)
supporting_evidence: Fama-regression tests addressing parameter instability and small-sample bias; medium/long-run UIP tests
contradicting_evidence: FX006 (curve factors predict); authors caution returns may be unpredictable
methodology: Fama (1984) regression re-examined; instability and bias corrections
sample_period: from mid-1980s (inflation result); post-ZLB period included
testability: Inflation-differential predictor is a separate, untested hypothesis for us
data_needed: CPI inflation for US/Japan/UK (ALFRED vintages for point-in-time US CPI; Japanese/UK vintages not yet sourced)
our_result: rate-differential trials killed; inflation-differential idea untested
publication_vs_sample: Published 2021/2022 inside our validation window; any test on 2015-2023 overlaps the authors' sample

citation: Lustig, Roussanov, Verdelhan (2011), Common Risk Factors in Currency Markets, Review of Financial Studies 24(11); NBER WP 14082
main_claim: A global 'slope' risk factor explains most of the cross-sectional variation in high- vs low-rate currency portfolio returns
mechanism: High-rate currencies load more on a global risk factor; carry is compensation for global risk, especially in bad times
methodology: Portfolio sorts on interest rates; factor model
limitations: Abstract only; return figures and sample not on the page; cross-sectional (many currencies), not single-pair
sample_period: not stated on the page read
testability: Not directly testable on one pair; motivates the single-pair caveat
our_result: single-pair carry killed (consistent with the caveat)

citation: Menkhoff, Sarno, Schmeling, Schrimpf (2012), Carry Trades and Global Foreign Exchange Volatility, Journal of Finance 67(2)
main_claim: High-rate currencies lose when global FX volatility rises unexpectedly; a volatility-risk proxy captures more than 90% of the cross-section of five carry portfolios
mechanism: Volatility risk premium; low-rate currencies hedge volatility shocks
supporting_evidence: Volatility proxy also prices US equity and corporate-bond cross-sections; liquidity risk matters less
methodology: Cross-sectional asset pricing with a global FX volatility proxy
limitations: Abstract only; a risk explanation, not a tested timing rule
sample_period: not stated on the page read
testability: Volatility-filtered carry (tested by us as V140)

citation: Chen, Tsang (2013), What Does the Yield Curve Tell Us About Exchange Rate Predictability?, Review of Economics and Statistics 95(1) 185-205, DOI 10.1162/REST_a_00231 (version read: author version June 2011)
main_claim: Relative Nelson-Siegel factors predict exchange-rate changes and excess currency returns 1-24 months ahead: a 1 pp rise in a country's relative slope or level factor is followed by ~3-4% annualised appreciation of its currency; a relatively steeper curve precedes depreciation
mechanism: Yield curves embed expectations of output and inflation; risk premia respond to them (asset-pricing view)
supporting_evidence: Monthly Aug 1985-Jul 2005 for CAD, GBP, JPY vs USD; corroboration 1991-May 2011; SPF survey correlations
contradicting_evidence: FX003; own rolling out-of-sample forecasts do not consistently beat a random walk or a single-maturity differential
methodology: Monthly regressions on relative Nelson-Siegel factors; small-sample inference corrections; rolling OOS (online appendix)
limitations: In-sample evidence; OOS weak by the authors' account; curvature least robust
data_needed: Zero-coupon or par yields US/Japan/UK (have US H.15, JGB MoF; UK not yet)
our_result: killed (V142 validation Sharpe 0.47 but in-sample -0.26; neighbour V141 negative)
publication_vs_sample: Sample ends 2005/2011; our in-sample 1991-2014 overlaps it; our validation 2015-2023 is after publication

citation: Neely, Weller, Ulrich (2009 journal; read: St. Louis Fed WP 2006-046B, rev. March 2007), The Adaptive Markets Hypothesis: Evidence from the Foreign Exchange Market
main_claim: FX technical-rule excess returns of the 1970s-80s were genuine, but filter and moving-average profits had disappeared by the early 1990s; less-studied rules declined but probably not completely
mechanism: Adaptive markets: learning and competition erode profitable rules
supporting_evidence: True out-of-sample tests of previously studied rules
contradicting_evidence: FX008 (cross-sectional momentum persists with limits to arbitrage)
limitations: Abstract and introduction only; high volatility limits precision
sample_period: 1970s onward (end date not on the pages read)
testability: Explains why no FX price-trend trial was pre-registered
publication_vs_sample: Decline documented after publication of the early studies (the point of the paper)

citation: Menkhoff, Sarno, Schmeling, Schrimpf (2012), Currency Momentum Strategies, Journal of Financial Economics 106(3)
main_claim: Cross-sectional currency momentum shows a winner-minus-loser spread of up to 10% p.a. that is hard to exploit because of very effective limits to arbitrage
mechanism: Under- and over-reaction; limits to arbitrage
supporting_evidence: Not explained by traditional risk factors; partly by transaction costs; distinct from carry

testability: Not testable with one or two pairs

citation: Burnside, Eichenbaum, Rebelo (2008), Carry Trade: The Gains of Diversification, Journal of the European Economic Association 6(2-3) 581-588
main_claim: Diversifying the carry trade across currencies boosts the typical Sharpe ratio by over 50% for a currency trader

sample_period: not stated on the page read

citation: Ranaldo, Söderlind (2007 WP; 2010 journal), Safe Haven Currencies, SNB Working Paper 2007-17
main_claim: Franc, euro, yen and pound tend to appreciate against the USD when US stocks fall, US bond prices rise and FX volatility rises, over hours to several days
supporting_evidence: WP sample 1993-2006; franc also appreciates against the other currencies; non-linear features

citation: Ito (2002), Is Foreign Exchange Intervention Effective?: The Japanese Experiences in the 1990s, NBER WP 8914
main_claim: Japanese interventions April 1991-March 2001 earned ~9 trillion yen, sold yen only below 125 and bought only above 125, were effective in the late 1990s; joint US-Japan operations were 20-50 times more effective
mechanism: Leaning against deviations from a long-run mean; coordination amplifies effect
supporting_evidence: Newly disclosed official data; profit calculations
methodology: Regressions of daily yen/dollar changes on intervention; profit accounting
limitations: Abstract only; disclosure date not on the page; data not observable in real time during the sample
